newsitem.title: UK: Nickel deficit due to end in 1996 - Brandeis.
newsitem.headline: Nickel deficit due to end in 1996 - Brandeis.

text.p: The large supply deficit in the nickel market is due to be eradicated this year as nickel demand has weakened on the back of softer stainless steel production and improved availability of stainless steel scrap, Robin Bhar of Brandeis Brokers Ltd said on Monday.

"Based on our view that the nickel market is likely to remain in balance over the next two years, total inventories are expected to fall only marginally but still stay relatively high at between 10 to 11 weeks," Bhar told the London Metal Exchange (LME) Metals Week seminar.
He forecast an average LME three-months nickel price of $7,826 a tonne in 1996, rising to $8,598 in 1997 and $9,370 in 1998.
In the immediate term, Bahr said, the great uncertainty is when the current de-stocking of stainless steel inventories will come to an end.
"It's very difficult to know whether we can end sooner or later, by the end of this year or in early 1997," Bhar said.
Stainless steel production accounts for two-thirds of nickel consumption.
Despite forecasting a balanced market for the next two years, Bhar cautioned that nickel is still instrinsically volitile and stable prices would be a surprise to most people.
"Price volitility should therefore remain a feature," he said.
He forecast that Russian exports to the West were expected to be around 156,000 tonnes this year, in line with previous years' levels.
Bhar forecast a four percent increase in nickel demand next year, and only a modest rebound in stainless steel production.
